presenterNotes: Encourage students to memorize the shapes of the four basic parent functions. Everything else is just a transformation.
The 'inside opposite, outside same' rule for horizontal vs. vertical shifts is crucial. Drill it with examples.
When combining transformations, have students identify the parent first, then list each transformation step by step.

A common mistake is confusing vertical stretch (narrower) with horizontal stretch (wider). Clarify that multiplying the whole function by a > 1 pulls points away from the x‑axis, making the graph appear narrower.

examples.prompt: The graph of a function is a V‑shape that opens upward with its lowest point at (0,0). What family does it belong to?
steps: Look at the shape: it's a V, not a straight line or U.
The absolute value parent function $ f(x) = |x| $ is V‑shaped.
Thus, the function belongs to the absolute value family.
examples.title: Example A – Identifying the Family

examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Look at the slope and y‑intercept. How does multiplying x by 2 and adding 1 change the graph?
examples.prompt: The function $ g(x) = 2x + 1 $ is a straight line. Explain to a partner how it differs from the parent $ f(x) = x $.
examples.title: Example B – Comparing a Function to Its Parent
steps: The parent linear function has slope 1 and passes through (0,0).
The 2 in $ g(x) $ makes the line steeper (slope 2).
The +1 shifts the line up by 1 unit.
So $ g $ is a transformation of the parent linear function.

examples.prompt: State the domain and range of the parent quadratic function $ f(x) = x^2 $.
steps: You can square any real number, so domain is all real numbers.
The output $ x^2 $ is never negative, so the smallest value is 0.
Range: $ y \ge 0 $.
examples.title: Example C – Domain and Range of a Parent Function

blocks.title: Identifying Parent Functions

questions.feedbackIfWrong: It is the absolute value function.
questions.prompt: The parent function of the family $ f(x) = |x| $ is called the ___ value function.
What is the parent function of $ g(x) = (x - 3)^2 $? (Use function notation, e.g., f(x)=x^2)

questions.feedbackIfWrong: A constant function is a horizontal line.
hints: It has the same y‑value for every x.
questions.prompt: The graph of a constant function is a ___ line.

confusionCorner.title: Parent vs. Transformed
confusionCorner.body: The parent function is the [[imp:simplest]] version — no numbers added, subtracted, or multiplied (except 1). If you see $ f(x) = x^2 + 3 $, the parent is $ x^2 $, not $ x^2 + 3 $. [[imp:Always strip away the extras to find the parent.]]

teacherCues: Sketch the graphs of $ y = x $, $ y = x^2 $, $ y = |x| $, and $ y = c $ on the board. Ask students to name each shape.
Ask: What is the simplest form of each type of function? That's the 'parent'.

explanation: A [[kw:parent function]] is the simplest function in a family of functions. It has no transformations applied.
Here are the most common parent functions:
• [[kw:Constant]]: $ f(x) = c $ — a horizontal line.
• [[kw:Linear]]: $ f(x) = x $ — a straight line through the origin with slope 1.
• [[kw:Absolute value]]: $ f(x) = |x| $ — a V‑shaped graph with vertex at the origin.
• [[kw:Quadratic]]: $ f(x) = x^2 $ — a U‑shaped parabola with vertex at the origin.
All other functions in each family are [[imp:transformations]] of the parent.

formulaCard.title: Parent Function Definitions
notes: The parent has no added constants or coefficients other than 1.
The graph passes through (0,0) except constant.
Knowing these shapes helps you quickly sketch more complex functions.
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Constant: } f(x) = c \quad \text{Linear: } f(x) = x $$ $$ \text{Absolute Value: } f(x) = |x| \quad \text{Quadratic: } f(x) = x^2 $$

discoveryHook.scenario: Think of parent functions as the plain‑vanilla versions of different families of functions. Just as all siblings share traits, all linear functions look like $ f(x) = x $ — just moved, stretched, or flipped. Recognizing these basic shapes is the key to understanding hundreds of more complicated graphs.

questions.prompt: Adding a constant to a function, like $ f(x) + 5 $, shifts the graph in which direction? (up or down)
hints: Positive outside means go positive direction.
Think of raising the whole graph.

questions.prompt: The graph of $ f(x - 7) $ is the graph of $ f(x) $ shifted ___ units to the right.
hints: Inside the function, the sign flips.

questions.prompt: Write the equation for the parent absolute value function shifted 2 units down. (Use function notation, e.g., f(x)=|x|-2)

examples.prompt: Graph $ g(x) = x - 4 $ and describe the transformation from the parent $ f(x) = x $.
examples.title: Example A – Graphing a Vertical Translation
steps: The parent is a line through (0,0) with slope 1.
$ g(x) = x - 4 $ has the same slope but y‑intercept -4.
The graph is the parent line shifted [[imp:4 units down]].

examples.prompt: Why does $ f(x + 2) $ shift the graph left, not right? Explain to a partner.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Try plugging in x = -2 into $ f(x+2) $. What value goes into f? What x gives the same output as the parent at x=0?
steps: In the parent $ f(x) $, the output at $ x = 0 $ is $ f(0) $.
In $ g(x) = f(x+2) $, to get that same output $ f(0) $, we need $ x+2 = 0 $, so $ x = -2 $.
Thus, the point that was at $ x=0 $ is now at $ x=-2 $ — a shift left.
This is why the direction is opposite the sign.
examples.title: Example B – Horizontal Shift Confusion

examples.prompt: Describe the transformation of $ h(x) = (x - 3)^2 + 1 $ from the parent $ f(x) = x^2 $.
steps: The $ -3 $ inside the square shifts the parabola [[imp:right 3 units]].
The $ +1 $ outside shifts it [[imp:up 1 unit]].
The vertex moves from (0,0) to (3,1). The shape stays the same.
examples.title: Example C – Combined Translation

blocks.title: Translations: Shifting Graphs

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine taking a paper cut‑out of a graph and sliding it around on a coordinate plane. That's a translation. Adding or subtracting outside the function moves it up/down; inside, left/right (but be careful — the sign flips!).

teacherCues: Write on the board: $ f(x) + k $ shifts up if $ k>0 $, down if $ k<0 $. $ f(x-h) $ shifts right if $ h>0 $, left if $ h<0 $.
Demonstrate with $ f(x) = x^2 $: graph $ (x-2)^2 $ and $ x^2 + 3 $.

explanation: A [[kw:translation]] shifts a graph horizontally, vertically, or both, without changing its size, shape, or orientation.
[[imp:Vertical translation]]: $ f(x) + k $ shifts the graph [[imp:up]] if $ k > 0 $, [[imp:down]] if $ k < 0 $.
[[imp:Horizontal translation]]: $ f(x - h) $ shifts the graph [[imp:right]] if $ h > 0 $, [[imp:left]] if $ h < 0 $. Notice the sign inside is opposite of the direction!
Example: $ g(x) = (x - 4)^2 $ is the parent $ f(x) = x^2 $ shifted 4 units to the right. The graph looks exactly like $ x^2 $ but moved.

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Vertical shift: } g(x) = f(x) + k $$ $$ \text{Horizontal shift: } g(x) = f(x - h) $$
notes: $ h > 0 $: right; $ h < 0 $: left (the sign inside flips!).
formulaCard.title: Translation Formulas

confusionCorner.body: $ f(x - h) $: if you see $ x - 3 $, the graph goes [[imp:right 3]]. If you see $ x + 3 $, it goes [[imp:left 3]]. Outside changes ($ +k $) go the way you'd expect. [[imp:Inside = opposite; Outside = same.]]
confusionCorner.title: Inside Changes Do the Opposite!

steps: The parent $ x^2 $ opens upward with vertex at (0,0).
The negative sign in front flips all y‑values: (1,1) becomes (1,-1); (2,4) becomes (2,-4).
The graph is a [[imp:reflection in the x‑axis]]; it opens downward.
examples.title: Example A – Reflecting a Quadratic
examples.prompt: Graph $ p(x) = -x^2 $ and describe the transformation from the parent $ f(x) = x^2 $.
Explain to a partner why $ f(x) = x^2 $ and $ g(x) = (-x)^2 $ look exactly the same.
steps: Because $ (-x)^2 = x^2 $, the function is unchanged.
Quadratics are even functions; they are symmetric about the y‑axis.
So a reflection over the y‑axis doesn't change the graph of an even function.
examples.title: Example B – Does $ f(-x) $ Always Look Different?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Square -x. What do you get? What kind of function is this?

steps: Reflection in x‑axis: put a negative in front: $ f(x) = -|x| $.
The graph is a V opening downward.
Range: $ y \le 0 $.
examples.prompt: Write the equation for the parent absolute value function reflected in the x‑axis. What is the new range?
examples.title: Example C – Reflecting an Absolute Value Function

discoveryHook.scenario: A reflection is like placing a mirror on an axis. The graph flips to the opposite side. If you put a negative sign in front of the whole function, the graph flips over the x‑axis (upside down). If the negative is inside with the x, it flips over the y‑axis (left‑right).

notes: Negative outside the function → flip over x‑axis.
Negative inside with x → flip over y‑axis.
A point $ (x, y) $ becomes $ (x, -y) $ (x‑axis) or $ (-x, y) $ (y‑axis).
formulaCard.title: Reflection Formulas

explanation: A [[kw:reflection]] flips a graph over a line called the line of reflection.
[[imp:Reflection in the x‑axis]]: $ g(x) = -f(x) $. Every y‑coordinate becomes its opposite. The graph flips upside down.
[[imp:Reflection in the y‑axis]]: $ g(x) = f(-x) $. Every x‑coordinate becomes its opposite. The graph flips left‑right.
Example: $ p(x) = -x^2 $ is the parent quadratic reflected in the x‑axis. It opens downward instead of upward.
The domain stays the same; the range may change (e.g., for $ -x^2 $, range is $ y \le 0 $).

blocks.title: Reflections: Flipping Graphs

questions.feedbackIfWrong: It's a reflection over the x‑axis.
questions.prompt: What transformation does $ g(x) = -f(x) $ represent? (Reflection over which axis? Answer: x-axis)
hints: The negative is outside the function.
It flips the graph upside down.
The negative sign in front flips the V.
It opens downward instead of upward.
questions.prompt: The graph of $ g(x) = -|x| $ is the parent absolute value graph reflected over the ___.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: It is reflected over the x‑axis.

hints: Reflection over y‑axis changes the sign of x.
questions.prompt: If the point (3, 4) is on $ f(x) $, what point is on $ g(x) = f(-x) $? (Answer like (-3,4))

teacherCues: Draw the parent $ y = x^2 $ and then $ y = -x^2 $. Ask: What happened? Where is the vertex now?
Show that $ -f(x) $ reflects over the x‑axis; $ f(-x) $ reflects over the y‑axis.

confusionCorner.title: Where Is the Negative?
confusionCorner.body: If the negative is [[imp:outside]] the function — like $ -f(x) $ — it's a vertical flip (over x‑axis). If it's [[imp:inside]] with the x — like $ f(-x) $ — it's a horizontal flip (over y‑axis). [[imp:Check the placement carefully!]]

questions.prompt: If $ f(x) = x^2 $, what transformation does $ g(x) = 4x^2 $ represent? (stretch or shrink)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: It's a vertical stretch by a factor of 4.

questions.prompt: A function multiplied by a factor between 0 and 1, like $ 0.3f(x) $, is a vertical ___.
The point (2, 4) on $ f(x) $ moves to (2, ?) on $ g(x) = 3f(x) $.

examples.title: Example A – Identifying a Stretch
examples.prompt: Compare the graphs of $ f(x) = |x| $ and $ g(x) = 3|x| $. Describe the transformation.
steps: The parent V has slopes -1 and 1.
In $ g(x) = 3|x| $, each y is tripled: (1,1) becomes (1,3); (-1,1) becomes (-1,3).
The V is [[imp:stretched vertically]] by a factor of 3. It's much steeper.

examples.title: Example B – Shrink vs. Stretch
steps: $ a = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 $, which is between 0 and 1.
Each y‑value is multiplied by 0.25, making them smaller.
The parabola becomes wider — this is a [[imp:vertical shrink]] by a factor of $ \frac{1}{4} $.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Compare $ a = \frac{1}{4} $ to 1. Is it greater than 1 or between 0 and 1? What happens to the y‑values?
examples.prompt: Explain to a partner whether $ g(x) = \frac{1}{4}x^2 $ is a stretch or a shrink.
Describe the transformation from $ f(x) = x^2 $ to $ g(x) = -2x^2 $.
steps: The negative sign reflects the parabola over the x‑axis (opens downward).
The 2 stretches it vertically by a factor of 2 (narrower).
So it's a reflection in the x‑axis followed by a vertical stretch.
examples.title: Example C – Reflection and Stretch

confusionCorner.body: Yes! A vertical stretch multiplies y‑values by a number greater than 1. The points are pulled away from the x‑axis, so the graph looks [[imp:narrower]] (or taller). A shrink brings them closer, making it look [[imp:wider]]. [[imp:Don't confuse 'stretch' with 'wider'!]]
confusionCorner.title: Stretch Makes It Narrower?

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine pulling a rubber graph up from the x‑axis. That's a vertical stretch. Pushing it toward the x‑axis is a vertical shrink. The factor tells you how much the y‑values are multiplied.

explanation: A [[kw:vertical stretch]] or [[kw:vertical shrink]] multiplies all y‑coordinates by a positive factor $ a $: $ g(x) = a \cdot f(x) $.
If $ a > 1 $, the graph is [[imp:stretched]] — it becomes narrower (points are pulled away from the x‑axis).
If $ 0 < a < 1 $, the graph is [[imp:shrunk]] — it becomes wider (points are pushed toward the x‑axis).
If $ a $ is negative, there is also a reflection. The stretch/shrink is by the absolute value of $ a $.
Example: $ g(x) = 2|x| $ doubles each y‑value; the V is steeper. $ h(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^2 $ halves each y‑value; the parabola is wider.

visuals.title: Vertical Stretch and Shrink
headers: Value of $ a $ in $ g(x) = a \cdot f(x) $

formulaCard.title: Stretch/Shrink Formula
notes: Multiply the y‑coordinate of the parent by $ a $.

blocks.title: Vertical Stretches and Shrinks
teacherCues: Draw $ y = x^2 $ and $ y = 2x^2 $ on the same axes. Point out that the 2 makes the parabola narrower.
Show $ y = \frac{1}{2}x^2 $ — wider. Multiply the y‑coordinate by a factor.
Write the order of operations for transformations on the board: 1. Horizontal shift, 2. Stretch/Shrink/Reflect, 3. Vertical shift. But focus on the overall effect.
Show $ g(x) = -2|x+3| + 1 $ and break it down: left 3, reflect + stretch, up 1.

discoveryHook.scenario: Real‑world graphs often combine several transformations. A dirt bike's height after jumping might be modeled by a transformed quadratic. By combining shifts, reflections, and stretches, we can model all kinds of situations.

questions.prompt: In $ g(x) = 2(x + 3)^2 - 5 $, what is the value of $ h $? (Remember the sign flip: if it's $ x+3 $, then $ h = -3 $)
hints: The form is $ f(x - h) $, so $ x + 3 = x - (-3) $.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: $ h = -3 $, indicating a left shift of 3.

hints: It's the coefficient multiplying the function.
It can also cause a reflection if negative.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The parameter $ a $ controls vertical stretch/shrink.
questions.prompt: The general transformation equation is $ g(x) = a \cdot f(x - h) + k $. The parameter that controls vertical stretch/shrink is ___.
Write the equation for the absolute value function shifted right 4, stretched by 2, and shifted up 1. (Use form a|x-h|+k)

examples.title: Example A – Breaking Down a Function
steps: Start with parent $ |x| $.
Horizontal: $ x - 1 $ → shift [[imp:right 1]].
Stretch/Reflect: $ a = -2 $ → [[imp:reflect]] over x‑axis and [[imp:stretch]] by factor 2.
Vertical: $ +4 $ → shift [[imp:up 4]].
Vertex moves from (0,0) to (1,4); V opens downward and is steeper.
examples.prompt: Describe all transformations from $ f(x) = |x| $ to $ g(x) = -2|x - 1| + 4 $.

steps: The function $ -2|x-1|+4 $: if you stretch $ |x| $ by 2 first, you get $ 2|x| $, then shift right 1 gives $ 2|x-1| $. That works.
But if you shifted first: $ |x-1| $, then stretched, you'd get $ 2|x-1| $. Same! For vertical stretches and horizontal shifts, order doesn't matter because they act on different axes.
However, when combining horizontal shifts and horizontal stretches, order matters. For our purposes, follow the form $ a \cdot f(x-h) + k $ and you'll be fine.
examples.prompt: Explain to a partner why the horizontal shift is applied before the vertical stretch.
examples.title: Example B – Order of Transformations
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Try doing the stretch first on $ |x| $, then shifting. Does it give the same result as shifting then stretching?

steps: Parent: $ f(x) = x^2 $.
Left 5: $ x + 5 $ inside → $ (x+5)^2 $.
Reflect + stretch by 3: $ a = -3 $ → $ -3(x+5)^2 $.
examples.title: Example C – Write an Equation from Description
examples.prompt: Write the equation of a quadratic function that has been shifted left 5, reflected over the x‑axis, stretched by 3, and shifted down 2.

confusionCorner.title: Parent Function First!
confusionCorner.body: Always start with the parent function in your mind. Apply transformations one at a time. [[imp:Horizontal shift → Stretch/Reflect → Vertical shift.]] Writing the function in the form $ a \cdot f(x-h) + k $ helps you see each piece clearly.

rows.1: Vertical stretch/shrink by $ |a| $; reflect if $ a<0 $

headers: Example in $ g(x) = a \cdot f(x-h) + k $
visuals.title: General Transformation Form

explanation: You can apply multiple transformations to a parent function. The general form for an absolute value or quadratic is: $$ g(x) = a \cdot f(x - h) + k $$
• $ h $: [[imp:horizontal shift]] (opposite sign).
• $ k $: [[imp:vertical shift]] (same sign).
• $ a $: [[imp:vertical stretch/shrink]] by $ |a| $, and [[imp:reflection]] if $ a < 0 $.
The order of operations inside the function matters, but you can think of the transformations happening from the inside out (horizontal first, then stretch/reflect, then vertical).
Example: $ g(x) = -\frac{1}{2}(x + 4)^2 - 3 $ — the parent $ x^2 $ is shifted left 4, reflected and shrunk by $ \frac{1}{2} $, and shifted down 3.

formulaCard.title: Combined Transformation Equation
notes: Stretch/shrink vertically by $ |a| $ and reflect if $ a < 0 $.
